Adames joins Aaron McKenna, who won the IBF title at Zuffa Boxing 10, as middleweight world champions under Zuffa control.Warburton is a step down in competition for Adames. Adames is far and away the best fighter Warburton has faced in his career.Warburton will enter Saturday's fight on a three-fight winning streak since a fourth-round TKO loss to Kieron Conway. It's unlikely Adames sticks at super middle, but it could be a bit of a glimpse into the future.
Adames is a better boxer, better puncher and more experienced at an elite level. Warburton has was stopped by Conway, who has just seven stoppage wins in 23 career victories, after Warburton's corner threw in the towel. There's no reason to expect Adames can't find the finish by attacking the body the same way Conway did. Pick: Carlos Adames via TKO5

body:
Nurmagomedov and Dvalishvili were also fined for the violent altercation
        
        
                                                                                                            
                                                    By
                                                
                                                            CBS Sports Staff

        Usman Nurmagomedov is facing six months in prison following the Wednesday incident in Abu Dhabi. Nurmagomedov, along with five others involved, will also have to pay a roughly $82,000 fine and be ordered to deportation following their prison terms for their part in the altercation that left Merab Dvalishvili battered and bloodied, according to a statement from the Abu Dhabi judicial department.Nurmagomedov and his associates approached Dvalishvili and his friend at the fighter hotel in Abu Dhabi ahead of Real American Freestyle wrestling event. Video appeared to show Nurmagomedov slap Dvalishvili before the brawl ensued.
All parties involved were immediately detained by authorities. RAF CEO and co-founder Chad Bronstein announced shortly after sentencing that Dvalishvili and his friend, Saba Lazishvili, had been released from police custody. Dvalishvili released a brief statement on social media on Friday to address the matter."Just want to let everyone know I have been released and I am good, healthy and ready to go. I want to thank everyone in Abu Dhabi for your help in resolving this matter," Dvalishvili wrote. "I love visiting Abu Dhabi and am happy to be welcomed. I do hope that they release everyone -- I would not press charges. I want peace and the best for all. Thanks everyone for your love and support."
Nurmagomedov is currently a free agent who was recently signed to the Professional Fighters League and, before that, Bellator. He has been seen at recent UFC events, supporting his brother, Umar Nurmagomedov, and teammate, Islam Makhachev.

title: Jerry Jones reveals when he thinks NFL expands to 18-game season, but process to get there is complicated - CBS Sports
description: Jones sees the NFL 'maybe' expanding to an 18-game regular season sooner than one might think
body:
Jones sees the NFL 'maybe' expanding to an 18-game regular season sooner than one might think
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Nov 13, 2026
                            
                    at
    3:36 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            3 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        The National Football League regular season could be expanding once again.From 1978 to 2020, the NFL played a 16-game regular season, but that changed in 2021 as the league expanded to a 17-game regular season. However, Dallas Cowboys owner Jerry Jones, one of the league's most influential voices, feels an expansion to an 18th regular-season game is just around the corner. "I don't think we're far away from it," Jones said Friday, via 105.3 The Fan in Dallas. "What is far away? Next month? No. Next year? Next year, maybe. Next year, maybe. That has to be negotiated with the players, but it's in everybody's best interest."Why would a greater physical toll in the regular season benefit the league's players playing one of the most violent sports? Jones claims the compromise would be to trim the NFL preseason once again. Teams typically play three exhibition games as a warm-up and to evaluate the back-end depth on their respective rosters. Two teams end up playing four preseason games if they participate in the "Hall of Fame Game" centered around the Pro Football Hall of Fame enshrinements in August.Jones feels simply erasing more preseason games and having the early regular season games, which already have a preseason feeling to them, is in everyone's best interest, players included. The NFL would certainly be in a position to ask for more money on its next media rights deals with its broadcast partners in that scenario. The league signed its current 11-year, $110 billion media rights deal with CBS, FOX, NBC, ESPN/ABC and Amazon Prime Video   in 2023. 
"You would cut back on the preseason games," Jones said. "You would have teams develop more in the first few games as the type of thing you're trying to get done in the preseason, but it's in everybody's interest. It certainly is in the player's best interest, in my mind, for sure. Having said that, I would anticipate that coming."Negotiating hurdles stand in way of any changeThe league's current CBA with the players' union is locked in through the 2030 season, so any tweaks to the regular season would necessitate additional negotiation between the league and the union. Commissioner Roger Goodell didn't see an 18-game regular season on the horizon like Jones does now when he addressed the topic at Super Bowl LX in February. "We have not had any formal discussions about it and frankly very little of any informal conversations," Goodell told reporters back in February. "It is not a given that we will do that. It's not something we assume will happen. It's something we want to talk about with the union leadership."  
One league source voiced concern to CBS Sports about increased injuries in an 18-game regular season in April. That is believed to be the biggest holdup to adding an additional regular-season game. "The bigger concern is now we're going to add another game, even if you multiply everything out with sensible assumptions, there are going to be more injuries," a league source told CBS Sports in April. "And it won't just be hamstrings. There are going to be season-enders and next-season-enders in Week 18 and 19. That's the biggest sticking point on the field."  One player, who requested anonymity, also told CBS Sports in April that some of the NFL's top stars could sit out games at the end of an extended 18-game season to charge up for the playoffs or to reduce the risk of injury. 
"The NFL's issue will be more related to getting top players to play in games beyond playoff contention, which I believe get exacerbated the more regular season games they play," the player told CBS Sports in April. "Top players will check themselves out more because games that don't matter late in the season will happen more often."While Jones has been able to bring many major changes to his Cowboys and the league at large over the years, an expansion to an 18-game regular season may be a little more complicated than he thinks.

    3:00 pm ET

        New Orleans Pelicans guard Dejounte Murray wants to be traded. A day after defending himself on social media in a now-deleted post that criticized his play during a 145-111 loss to the Brooklyn Nets earlier this week, the former All-Star and his representatives are "working on a resolution" for his exit from the franchise, ESPN reported Friday. One team that has "registered interest" in adding Murray is the Phoenix Suns, per Chris Haynes. ProPelsTalk, a Pelicans podcast, posted clips on social media highlighting purported mistakes Murray made during his team's fourth consecutive loss, to which Murray responded that fans have "no f--- ing clue what we are dealing with.""Ohhhhh let's talk about it," Murray posted in a now-deleted tweet. "When you run post plays, are they suppose to catch on the block or the 3pt line? Let's hear it Mr social media coach, Gm and President? You have no f---ing clue what we dealing with. Maybe you should ask the whole team individually how they feel on a serious note and then pull rethink alot of shit."Murray finished with five points, four assists, and two rebounds in 28 minutes during the loss. This season, Murray is averaging 13.4 points, the lowest since his third season in the league with the San Antonio Spurs. On the same day Murray tweeted and then deleted that tweet, he also responded to another tweet, noting that the Pelicans are 1-8 with Murray and 3-0 without him.
"From what's going on INSIDE, this sounds like someone hit you to say this!!" Murray wrote in a now-deleted tweet. "THE 'SABOTAGE' IS REAL!!"Murray appeared in just 14 games during the 2025-26 season after recovering from a torn Achilles that sidelined him for more than a year. The Athletic's Sam Amick reported on Thursday that he expects the Pelicans to have "very legitimate conversations" about Murray being moved."Dejounte (Murray), I would fully expect to have very legitimate conversations about him being on the move," Amick said. I thought that would be the case closer to the deadline. The mood certainly is the type of thing that could accelerate it."
Murray, 30, is in the final guaranteed season of his current contract. He has a player option for $30.7 million for the 2027-28 season.

title: Mauricio Pochettino leaves incomplete legacy as USMNT tenure nears finish - CBS Sports
description: While he raised daily standards and brought along a promising young core, failing to win a Concacaf trophy and ex
body:
While he raised daily standards and brought along a promising young core, failing to win a Concacaf trophy and exiting the World Cup in the round of 16 leaves an undeniable feeling of unfinished business
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Nov 13, 2026
                            
                    at
    2:29 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            6 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        He raised the standard of U.S. Soccer. It's the first thing that you hear from multiple people as Mauricio Pochettino prepares to oversee his final two games. The reality is more mixed. His 1.91 points per game are the third-best of any manager to oversee the United States men's national team for more than 10 games, behind Gregg Berhalter and Bruce Arena, but he's also the first permanent manager since Steve Sampson to not win a Concacaf title, with the USMNT falling short in both the Concacaf Nations League and the Concacaf Gold Cup. That said, it's hard to say that he isn't leaving the USMNT in a better place than he found it, although some credit should be given to U.S. Soccer and former sporting director Matt Crocker for that. It's a conflicted legacy that Pochettino will leave, but it's also one that can't be fully realized until after he oversees his final two matches against Haiti. If his departure overshadows the performance on the pitch, leaving the USMNT without a chance to win the Concacaf Nations League final for a second consecutive tournament, that will undo a significant portion of the good that he has accomplished by bringing along younger members of the squad. But as he prepares to depart, the USMNT exited the World Cup in the round of 16, the same stage as in 2022, and questions remain about how they'll hold up against the world's top teams. With the 2028 Olympics coming up and a new training facility that allows space for the youth and senior sides to train in the same place, alongside the improvement in U.S. youth development thanks to MLS Next and MLS Next Pro, the USMNT were going to be in a good place no matter who took over at this stage, which is also what makes it critical to look at what comes next.  Haiti vs. USMNT: How to watch Date: Saturday, Nov. 14 | Time: 4:30 p.m. ET Location: Nu Stadium -- Miami, Florida TV: TNT | Live stream: HBO Max Odds: Haiti +750; Draw +440; USMNT -350  Why the USMNT job remains attractive "Our ambition is high, and we believe that this is one of the great coaching jobs in the world. We have an experienced group of players; we've got a dynamic young pool of players," U.S. Soccer CEO JT Batson said. "Last night, Mauricio, staff, and most of the men's team watched our U-20s play here at the national training center, which was a pretty special moment. We publicly shared our ambition is to be in a position where we're winning major tournaments, including World Cups, and we want to make sure that we're attracting leaders who help us do just that. We know from our experience that great leaders want to work with great people, and great leaders want to make an impact on things that matter, and we think that we've proven at U.S. Soccer that we're a great place to work and we're a great place to make legacy-defining impact." 
Call it What You Want: A weekly podcast where Jimmy Conrad, Charlie Davies and Tony Meola cover all things USMNT and the state of the beautiful game in the United States. Catch the show YouTube live every Tuesday and Friday at 10 a.m. ET.    U.S. Soccer is still in talks to hire a director of soccer who will work with the incoming head coach, United States women's national team coach Emma Hayes and the rest of the U.S. Soccer staff to shape the vision of American soccer. The sport is growing rapidly here, which is what makes this such an attractive job even without the shine of hosting a men's World Cup on home soil to add to the sales pitch. Listening to Batson, while BJ Callaghan may be one of the top American fits for the role, you can easily see why the USMNT would like to bring in Pep Guardiola if they can, and there's a sales pitch there to at least get top targets to pick up the phone. Pochettino's incomplete legacyThis doesn't diminish what Pochettino has done while leading the national team, but each manager has made his mark on American soccer in his own way. Jurgen Klinsmann added legitimacy to the USMNT role and ushered in an era of German Americans who led the squad to new heights. Gregg Berhalter came in, raised the floor for the squad, did excellent work with dual-national recruitment and led the squad out of its group at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar. Sure, in hindsight, things should've ended there, with U.S. Soccer moving in a different direction after the World Cup, but the players also wanted continuity. 
You can make the same argument that Pochettino maybe shouldn't have been signed to a new contract following the World Cup, but even he seemed to believe that an opportunity such as Manchester United wouldn't have come this quickly. If he were leaving in 2028, after Steve Cherundolo led the U.S. U-23s on a strong run in the Olympics, the departure wouldn't be as bittersweet as this one, which feels like a job left unfinished by the Argentine.  Carrying Poch's standard forwardPochettino did add confidence, and to hear players like Sebastian Berhalter, Cavan Sullivan, Alex Freeman and Neil Pierre, among others, tell it, when Pochettino was at his best, this team would press anyone off the pitch. Now the onus is on the players to take that forward under new management. "I think Poch definitely raised the standard since he's been in charge. I think you guys have seen that, just the intensity of training, how we approach games, he's changed our way of thinking as players, from calling the friendlies that we have in certain camps official games, not official games. He wants us to just be of a mindset to go out there and win," Folarin Balogun said. 
"He's laid the foundation, and I think we, as players, have that ownership to not just do that because Poch was in charge; I think we have the ownership as players to carry that out because we know the standard," he continued. "So yeah, I think that's the benefit of having a top coach, and I'm sure you know whether he's here or not, the US will look to replace him with another top coach." A tearful Pochettino and the disappointed players show that this didn't end the way anyone would've wanted, but that doesn't mean there isn't plenty of good to build on for whoever comes next. With Cherundolo leading the December camp, there's plenty of time to ensure that the next hire is the right one, but now that U.S. Soccer has shown that it can recruit a coach of Pochettino's caliber, there's no reason to stop there. Having a coach coveted by others is a product of success, but having a system that can move past that proves things are sustainable. The word "sustainable" hasn't been one that U.S. Soccer has been able to use as of late, as one thing going wrong could lead to a spiral, but with benefactors, facilities and youth all at once, it's time to build a future that isn't dependent on who the coach is, because that's what will lead to winning a World Cup.

        It's Week 10 of the 2026 NFL season, and the trade deadline is officially behind us. We saw the Jaguars go all in, the Vikings add a familiar face in QB Kirk Cousins and the Bears land Jeffery Simmons. Some players will make their debuts on their new teams in an exciting week for the league.As we go down the stretch of the regular season, these games each mean more and more, and we have some big ones coming up. While some are obvious matchups to circle on the schedule, there are a few that are flying under the radar but could turn out to be a great watch.Here is a look at three games you should keep an eye on this weekend:Texans vs. Browns Sunday, Nov. 15 at 1 p.m. ET on FOX (Stream on fubo, try for free)Browns quarterback Deshaun Watson is set to return after missing last week due to a concussion, and the return holds more significance than normal. Watson is facing his former team, the Houston Texans, who drafted him at No. 12 overall in 2017 and where he stayed until 2021. The Cleveland Browns (5-4) are the first team outside the playoff bubble, sitting at No. 9, and the Houston Texans (3-5) are No. 11 in the AFC. According to CBS Sports projections, if the Browns lose, their playoff chances drop to 19.0%, and a win puts their playoff chances up to 52.6%. If the Texans lose, their postseason odds drop to 16.75%, while a win would put them at 50.1%.
The AFC North is in a tight race, and this game could be big for the Browns' standings. This matchup intrigues me because these two teams have potential, aren't quite out of the race but are long shots, and are finding their identities. The offense vs. defense matchups also make this game a fun one to watch.The Texans are third in passing yards per game at 296.4 and face a Browns defense that has allowed the sixth-fewest passing yards per game at 201.0. The Browns offense is among the bottom in rushing yards, and the Texans defense is in the top half in terms of rushing yards allowed, so the run game could be a major factor in who wins here. Another mismatch is the Browns' struggling offensive line and the Texans' ability to generate sacks. Houston had eight sacks last week, tying a franchise record.
Houston quarterback C.J. Stroud is coming off a huge win, tying a career-high with five touchdowns, while the Browns are looking to snap a two-game losing streak. Raiders vs. SeahawksSunday, Nov. 15 at 4:05 p.m. ET on CBS, streaming on Paramount+In the last few hours of the trade deadline, the Raiders traded Cousins to the Vikings after nine starts and a 4-5 record. He finished his time with Vegas this season with 2,340 yards, 20 touchdowns and eight interceptions. With Cousins in Minnesota, first-overall pick Fernando Mendoza will get his first NFL start. This game marks the beginning of what should be a lengthy Mendoza Era in Las Vegas, and it will be interesting to see how Mendoza comes out. The Seahawks defense won't make it easy, though; they are at the top of the league, allowing the fewest passing yards (155.1) and the fewest total yards allowed (244.2).
The Raiders offense has been moving the ball, at least in the air, landing fifth in passing yards per game (259.7). Their run game is what they need to improve on, as it's second worst in the league in yards per game (71.3).The run game will be crucial this week, especially with what they're dealing with at QB. Sam Darnold is sidelined, leaving Drew Lock to run things for a second straight week, but he is dealing with an oblique/elbow injury himself. His injury could mean Seattle leans more toward the run, something that hasn't been their strongest offensive element. They have a defensive mismatch on their side, since the Raiders' defense has allowed the most rushing yards per game (151.2).Steelers vs. BengalsSunday, Nov. 15 at 8:20 p.m. ET on NBC (Stream on fubo, try for free)This game is big in terms of divisional standings and the playoff picture, but these are two teams who haven't received as much attention as some of the other AFC heavy hitters.
The Steelers and Bengals are both 6-2, but Pittsburgh has the edge in the division and the top spot thanks to a 2-1 record among AFC North teams, compared to Cincinnati's 1-1 record. This is their second meeting of the year, and with such a close race, their head-to-head record could be the difference maker when it comes to crowning a divisional champ. The Steelers won their last meeting, a close one, 30-27. I expect this game to be an exciting, close matchup as well.Both are playoff teams right now, with the Steelers currently occupying the No. 4 seed and the Bengals at No. 6, and both teams are currently in four-game win streaks. One of those streaks will have to come to an end this week, though.
These teams are coming off very different weeks. The Steelers return from a bye, while the Bengals are coming off an international game in Madrid. This game will be one that's looked back on as crucial for both teams this season, and with so much on the line, this game should be one you watch this week.

With the championship match set for D.C., Trinity Rodman and company can secure a home final if they can halt an underdog Utah squad riding high after stunning San Diego

        The NWSL playoffs roll on with the semifinal round, and fans will be treated to a glimpse of the future site of the 2026 NWSL Championship. Audi Field in Washington, D.C., has a way of making regular-season games feel even bigger, and on Saturday it hosts another penultimate chapter ahead of the final.This will be the third home semifinal at Audi Field in as many years, and the third-place Washington Spirit will host the eighth-place Utah Royals (on CBS, noon ET), with a chance to play at home in the NWSL Championship on Nov. 21. A neutral site is chosen for the NWSL Championship annually, and this year's Audi Field announcement was made back in June, setting in motion endless possibilities for the Washington Spirit to have an all-home playoff run.But they're going up against the breakout team of the year in the Utah Royals, a team that finished in 12th place last season, with only six wins. Now they've spent the 2026 regular season creating new club history and are coming off a huge quarterfinal upset over the second-place San Diego Wave.Here's everything to know about the big game:Playoffs run through Washington SpiritThe Spirit's long season had highs, some lows and plenty of plateaus. While the Spirit at one point looked like prime contenders for the NWSL Shield, they let it slip away to eventual winners Gotham FC with two games remaining in the season.
But the NWSL playoffs are a different beast. A three-game gauntlet to claim the big prize, where the only real thing that matters is the best form over a short span of matches. There's no better time to make a statement than the quarterfinal round, and both the Spirit and Utah delivered.The Spirit's 4-1 demolition of the Portland Thorns was a showcase of their skill, but also of how the group is fueled and functions at home. Trinity Rodman scored twice and added an assist, as Portland were outclassed on the pitch between their giveaways and the Spirit's breakaway chances."They're steaming now. They're going now, which is obviously what you want. A team that starts really high performing in the playoffs," Utah head coach Jimmy Coenraets said about the Spirit.
"I think the biggest difference is that you go to Rowdy Audi, which I think, looking at the Portland [quarterfinal], within two minutes it scored two goals based on just the whole crowd getting behind them. So I think it's being smart about momentum, it's being smart about timing and stuff. Maybe sometimes killing the game slightly more, and then just being smart about a few things."Rodman is the headliner of the Spirit's roster. She finished the regular season with a career-best 12 goals and eight assists, was named an NWSL MVP finalist this year and has carried that form into the postseason. A massive bright spot for the Spirit is also the overall player depth.Despite player movement and injuries, the group seems to be hitting its stride in the playoffs, especially with newcomers Melissa Bethi and Clara Lavunga, who joined midseason. Both players scored in the quarterfinal and could prove to be the difference-makers for the Spirit after three consecutive semifinal appearances. Alongside other players who are now staples of the club -- defender Tara Rudd and midfielder Andi Sullivan, the longtime team captain -- the group is not trying to get ahead of itself with the possibility of playing a championship at home. First, the Spirit have to tackle the semifinal.
"I can't even go there in my mind. Like, you know, everyone's talking about the final being here, but again, we have a semifinal, so you can't get to there yet. But obviously, we want to be there, so that's definitely motivation to get the job done," Sullivan said on "Attacking Third." 
"The rotations of players coming in and out, and whether that's due to injuries or new signings or whatever it may be, and I just think that's a testament to, like, the locker room and the closeness we have in the locker room ... and I think that's what we're really like leaning on into this playoff push."Utah Royals' successful turnaroundClubs hoping to change their fortunes will look to Utah as a blueprint. After a 6-13-7 record and 12th-place season last year, and 11th place in 2024, the group is now navigating its first-ever playoff appearance.
Head coach Jimmy Coenraets, who was recently nominated for NWSL coach of the year, had been the interim coach before taking over the team permanently in October 2024. Mina Tanaka's more elevated play, along with the return of veterans like Cloe Lacasse and Paige Monaghan, helped turn the page for Utah in 2026. Signing Miyabi Moriya and Kiana Palacios and trading for Narumi Miura were also key offseason moves.While the group spent the second half of the season winning one week and losing the next, the playoffs offered a reset. With locker-room belief and a "why not us?" attitude as the eighth-seeded playoff team, Utah delivered the biggest upset of the postseason with a cagey 1-0 win against the second-place San Diego Wave. It was Palacios who provided the game-winning goal, after receiving the setup from Lacasse. 
Goalkeeper Mandy McGlynn is also on fire for the Royals. She racked up crucial saves throughout the quarterfinal and is rallying the team into D.C. She has previous experience winning the 2023 NWSL Championship with the former eighth-place Gotham FC side. Coenraets believes her experience and the team's camaraderie on the road will be huge in Saturday's mental test.
"I think that's how you create your own momentum. So when you're going against, I don't know how many it will be, 20,000, 22,000 [at Audi], you have to ... like it's impossible to cancel the noise, but you just got to create your own noise. You've got to make sure that players feel the energy from the sideline, from players and staff. I think that's the biggest message, because again, it will be loud, and I have to say I was impressed last week listening to [how] loud they were. But again, like you have an opportunity to create your own momentum, and I think that's what we want to do tomorrow," he said.What's nextThe Washington Spirit will host the Utah Royals at Audi Field in Washington, D.C., on Saturday. The winner of Saturday's semifinal will face the winner of Sunday's semifinal between Gotham FC and the Kansas City Current. The final two teams will face off in the NWSL Championship on Nov. 21 on CBS.

NEW YORK -- As Kayla Harrison closes in on the biggest fight of her career on Saturday in arguably the most prestigious women's matchup in the sport's history, it's difficult for her not to reflect back upon the battle that led up to it. Harrison (19-1), the 36-year-old UFC bantamweight champion, will take on former champion and teammate Amanda Nunes (23-5), the greatest female fighter of all time, in the co-main event of UFC 334 inside Madison Square Garden. The fight was originally scheduled for January at UFC 324 until Harrison withdrew just 11 days before. After years of competing through herniated discs in her neck dating back to her days as a two-time U.S. Olympic gold medalist in judo, Harrison suffered an injury in training so severe that it required immediate surgery. And her road to rehabilitation was so daunting and painful that she battled with the possibility that a full recovery might not be in the cards. "It was a wrench that I was not expecting in the plans, but God is good," Harrison told CBS Sports on Tuesday. "The recovery was a lot harder than I anticipated, so I'm very grateful to be here this week. I have been humbled and I'm hungry. I'm hungrier than I think I have been in a long time. I have no doubt that it all happened for a reason. Who I am as a result of that hurdle and obstacle in my life has propelled me to even greater heights as a person, as a mother and as a fighter. I'm excited to showcase it."
As Harrison put it, the physical trials she endured throughout her recovery left her in a position to really question how badly she wanted to come back for what might prove to be the final bout of her eight-year pro MMA career. Harrison hasn't yet ruled either way, but has maintained that the end is near, and that a retirement after Saturday for her, win or lose, remains a possibility.For as much as Nunes, the only female two-division champion in UFC history who went on to defend both titles simultaneously, will need to shake off three years of cage rust following her 2023 retirement due to physical burnout, Harrison will be returning to the Octagon for the first time in 17 months since submitting Julianna Pena in June 2025 at UFC 316 to win the 135-pound title. 
A native of Middletown, Ohio, who now lives and trains in South Florida, Harrison said that the prospect of finally facing off against Nunes is the only reason she endured the recovery from neck surgery to put on the gloves one more time. Had her injury postponed an upcoming fight against anyone else, she would've walked away for good. The reason is simple. From the first time she set foot inside an MMA gym in late 2016, Harrison maintained she was only entering the sport to become the best to ever do it. By the time she made her pro debut in 2018 as a teammate of Nunes at American Top Team in Coconut Creek, Florida, "The Lioness" was months away from knocking out Cris Cyborg in the biggest fight in women's MMA history and cementing her status as the GOAT.So, should Harrison defeat Nunes, the GOAT, on Saturday in a long-awaited matchup that has been talked about for so many years (and led to Nunes leaving ATT in early 2022), a victory would make Harrison what? 
"The GOAT," Harrison said. "I mean, I think so."
Not every historian will completely agree. For as unique as her career has been, whether it was winning a pair of 155-pound tournaments (and $1 million prizes) with the PFL or the three wins she has recorded as a bantamweight since making her UFC debut in 2024, Harrison doesn't have anywhere near the number of legendary names on her resume akin to Nunes.What Harrison has been, however, is completely dominant, winning 19 of her 20 pro fights, with the only defeat – a five-round unanimous decision to Larissa Pacheco in the finals of the 2022 PFL lightweight tournament – coming on an off night to an opponent she had soundly defeated twice in the previous three years. "I have come to peace with my career," Harrison said. "It's something that I really had to wrestle with when I was recovering from the injury, not knowing if this fight was ever going to happen. I'm at peace with my career and happy with everything. Six-year-old me could never have dreamed of this life that I live. I am eternally grateful and this is the fight that I have wanted since I started MMA.
"A lot of things had to go right in order for this to happen, and some things did go wrong and it's still happening. I'm grateful to Amanda and I just feel really blessed. When you look at my life, sometimes I can't believe it. I really can't. It has been full of a lot of lows but so many more highs. And to be the GOAT, that was the goal from Day 1."Harrison's personal story has long been one about perseverance. Abused by her judo coach as a youth, she went on to raise awareness as an advocate for child sexual abuse. She also became a single mother after adopting her niece and nephew and serves as their homeschool teacher. Harrison's life of sacrifice extends to her unique fighting legacy when you factor in the seemingly insurmountable weight cut she was forced to make to realize her UFC dreams. 
After competing in judo on the Olympic level at 172 pounds, Harrison initially cut down to 155 pounds to compete as a lightweight with PFL. But the UFC folded its 145-pound featherweight division following Nunes' retirement, which meant Harrison needed to cut an additional 20 pounds to make the bantamweight. The fact that Harrison successfully did so even once shows how badly becoming a UFC champion has been part of her professional dreams. On Friday, she will attempt to make 135 pounds for the fourth time in a grueling process that demands every ounce of her discipline and commitment.  
"I don't know if you can ever master cutting weight," Harrison said. "I don't know if that's ever a thing. But I do have a remarkable team behind me. This has been the 'least stressful' weight cut so far, but it is what it is."
Both Harrison and Nunes didn't have a bad word to say about each other for the vast majority of the fight's promotion, as both appear to have decided that any lingering negativity that may or may not have fueled Nunes' ATT exit some five years into their tenure as teammates isn't worth rehashing. Many of their former coaches and teammates, however, tell a different story. "We only sparred one time. It was before I had [officially] moved to American Top Team and I hadn't had a fight yet," Harrison said. "I had been training for a couple months, and I was trying out different gyms. My second day [at ATT] was sparring day with Amanda."So, what happened in the sparring match? "No, no, that's a faux pas," Harrison said. "We don't talk about what happened in sparring. But, I mean, clearly I had never fought before. It's not like I walked in there and absolutely thrashed her."
Harrison was often asked, even before her pro debut, by media members whether she would ever want to fight Nunes. Each and every time, Harrison said yes. "I think that was probably what rubbed Amanda the wrong way," Harrison said. "I wasn't bringing it up, but I would say, 'Of course I would want to fight her. She's the greatest of all time.' To me, that's a compliment. If [UFC bantamweight and teammate] Bea [Mesquita] does an interview and says she wants to fight me, I don't take that as a threat. I take that as a compliment. Of course, you should want to fight me."Harrison remains steadfast that she never looked at their training relationship as anything but a chance to make each other better. Still, the two eventually stopped working together once Harrison began establishing herself as a dominant pro fighter, and most still believe that Harrison's presence had a lot to do with Nunes' eventual decision to start her own gym.  
"You have to ask Amanda that. I'm not in her head," Harrison said. "We don't talk about it, and it's not like I'm texting her about it. I was very much a team player. I never felt threatened or that there was a scarcity of coaches. That's one of the reasons that I trained there, because of her. If you want to be the best, you have to train with the best. By the time I got to work with her, it was a great opportunity for me. I feel like we are both very respectful, and it never got nasty. "I have nothing bad to say about Amanda, but I'm just a loyal person. I started my career at ATT and I'm going to end my career at ATT. The same four guys are going to be in my corner on Saturday night, as they were on my first fight and I'm happy with that."At Thursday's final press conference, the mask of restraint previously worn by Harrison and Nunes finally came off as the two engaged in an extended argument about why their training relationship fell apart. Nunes accused Harrison of not being honest about wanting to fight her from the beginning and Harrison ended the public spat by declaring that their ATT coaches only separated them from training with one another because "they were trying to protect you from me." 
Quoting her longtime judo coach, Jimmy "Big Jim" Pedro Sr., Harrison believes Saturday's fight is a battle between a racehorse and a workhorse or, in fight terms, a classic matchup between a powerful striker and a grinding wrestler. "I think we are so different as fighters, even in our training method," Harrison said. "She is wicked talented, very gifted. She's a thoroughbred and I'm a workhorse. She has amazing knockouts and great highlights and I'm more of a gritty, grind-it-out type fighter. So, it's kind of a classic matchup in that sense but it ends with my hand raised."Who wins Gane vs. Hokit, and how exactly does the fight end? Visit SportsLine now to get detailed picks and analysis from the incomparable expert who is up over $21,000 on his UFC picks since May 2018, and find out.

        Now in his 32nd season, Michigan State coach Tom Izzo has earned a No. 1 seed for the NCAA Tournament four times in his career, but it has only happened once since 2001 and not at all since 2012. Could this be the year that changes?After beating Duke in the Champions Classic on Tuesday night, the Spartans are on a strong early trajectory. With star point guard Jeremy Fears Jr. leading the way, Michigan State could be gearing up for a special season.Purdue and Michigan will be struggling to meet their recent standards this season, opening the door for Michigan State to dominate the Big Ten as it did in the 2024-25 season. The Spartans earned a No. 2 seed that season after going 17-3 in the league. However, they didn't have a nonconference victory nearly as valuable as their 2026-27 win over Duke will be.
        
            
                Dismantling of Duke by Michigan State shows it might be time to recalibrate expectations for Blue Devils
                
                    Isaac Trotter                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
The Blue Devils have slipped to No. 2 seed in our first in-season Bracketology update. Duke is still beloved by predictive metrics and is in line for another great season, but the Michigan State loss showed that it's a work in progress.

Well, the Bruins proved they deserve to be much higher — for now anyway — when they beat Arizona 84-75 on the season's first night. After that win and two subsequent buy-game wins, the 3-0 Bruins are up to a No. 4 seed in our update. The remainder of UCLA's nonconference schedule is relatively light, but the Arizona win should stand the test of time.Why isn't UCLA ahead of Arizona? Well, the Wildcats still rank ahead of UCLA in predictive metrics and have huge opportunities against Auburn and UConn coming over the next week. But the Wildcats did drop from a No. 1 seed to a No. 2 seed in this projection. We'll learn more about Tommy Lloyd's club very soon.
While UCLA stands out as a big riser from the Big Ten, Purdue stands out for the opposite reason. After debuting in the preseason as a No. 5 seed, the Boilermakers started 1-2 with losses to Gonzaga and Valparaiso. Purdue is now one of the "Last Four in" and slotted as a No. 12 seed being sent to the "Opening Round." Why didn't they fall out entirely? They are still a top-40 team in predictive metrics, suggesting that a rebound is likely in the cards.Rematch rulesAmid conference consolidation and tournament expansion, the NCAA has again relaxed rules around rematches. Official NCAA guidance no longer includes a mandate to avoid nonconference rematches in the second round.While the NCAA will seek to avoid nonconference rematches in the Opening Round and first round, those rules can be relaxed for conferences with more than nine teams in the field. They can also be relaxed if a league has multiple teams among the final 12 at-large teams playing in the Opening Round.
This is how we ended up with the possibility of a first-round game between Tennessee and Florida State. The Volunteers and Seminoles play on Dec. 1, meaning the committee will seek to avoid a potential first-round matchup between them. But the SEC has 13 teams in this projection, and the ACC has two teams playing in the Opening Round.To avoid violating other bracketing principles, it was easier just to roll with a potential Tennessee/FSU rematch. As for conference rematches, they are allowed to occur as early as the second round between teams that played only once before the NCAA Tournament. But even that can be relaxed for leagues with nine or more teams in the bracket, which the Big 12, Big Ten and SEC each have in this projection. Full conference breakdownHere is the full rundown of multi-bid leagues from the latest 76-team CBS Sports Bracketology.
